messages.subject: Estimated survival curve from the Cox model
messages.subject_clean: Estimated survival curve from the Cox model
messages.body_plain:
I am fitting a Cox regression on a simulated data, I have included the code below. Is there a command in INLA to get the estimated survival at each timepoint after fitting the Cox model?
Thank you,
Georgiana

#Cox regression ;
alpha=1.5
n=200
eta = 1
lambda = exp(eta)
y = rweibull(n, shape= alpha, scale= lambda^(1/-alpha))
event = rep(1,n)
data= list(y=y, event=event, x=x)
#fit Cox model in INLA and get estimated survival

formula = inla.surv(y, event) ~ 1
resultcox = inla(formula, family = "coxph", data = data)
resultcoximpr=inla.hyperpar(resultcox)
summary(resultcoximpr)

messages.subject: Prediction by INLA
messages.body_plain:
I am aware that, in INLA there is no function ``predict'' as for glm/lm in R. Predictions must to done as a part of the model fitting itself, see:
http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-How-can-I-do-predictions-using-INLA-

But this has a huge drawback as each time when you do prediction, you have to fit the model, which is not efficient, especially when you have to do prediction sequentially. I wonder if there is any new development on INLA that makes prediction more convenient, like that for glm/lm in R. Thanks a lot!

-Thomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi Thomas,

to the best of my knowledge there is not yet an easy/automatic way to process data sequentially using INLA. However, I think there is some development in this direction, see for example

https://www.scss.tcd.ie/disciplines/statistics/statica/statica_web/Zurich_11.pdf

but I am not sure what the current state of this proposal is and whether it is applicable in the general context.

Best,
Andrea

messages.subject: GLMM with random slope coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Hope someone can help with the following question. For a study on animal preferences I would like to fit a GLMM with random slope coefficients. There are multiple observations per individual. Searching the web and this group I believe the code should be like:

f(animal_id, covariate, model=”iid”)

Below some simulation code and the INLA model results. The fixed effect parameters look OK. Since the random effect of the slope parameters are defined as rnorm(…,0,1), I would expect the precision hyper parameters to be ~1, but in almost all cases they are <<1. I tried some alternative priors, but that doesn’t seem to change much.

Does anyone has an idea why the precision parameter estimates seem to be different from 1? Or do I miss-specify the model or  miss-interpreted the results?

And a side question: Any suggestions on what would be the most appropriate prior distribution for the example below is very much appreciated.

Thanks in advance,

Cheers, Geert

library(INLA)

library(splines)

beta=c(-3,3,-3,3)

xseq<-seq(0,1,by=0.01)

plot(xseq,bs(xseq,4,intercept=F)%*% beta,type="l",lwd=2,col="red")

N_animals=100

N_obs=100

for (i in 1:N_animals){

b=rnorm(4,0,1)

lines(xseq,bs(xseq,4,intercept=F)%*% (beta+b),type="l")

x<-runif(N_obs,0,1)

X<-bs(x,4,intercept=F)

colnames(X)<-paste("X",1:4,sep="")

lp<--3 + X %*% (beta + b)

mu<-exp(lp)/(1+exp(lp))

y<-rbinom(N_obs,1,mu)

d<-cbind(data.frame(id=rep(i,N_obs),y=y,x=x,b=rep(b,N_obs)),X)

if (i==1) alld<-d

else alld<-rbind(alld,d)

}

alld$id4<-alld$id3<-alld$id2<-alld$id1<-alld$id

formula = y ~ X1+X2+X3+X4+f(id1,X1,model="iid",prior="normal",param=c(1,0.001))+f(id2,X2,model="iid",prior="normal",param=c(1,0.001))+f(id3,X3,model="iid",prior="normal",param=c(1,0.001))+f(id4,X4,model="iid",prior="normal",param=c(1,0.001))

mod.seeds = inla(formula,data=alld,family="binomial",Ntrials=1)

> Hi,

> Searching the web and this group I believe the code should be like:

>
> Below some simulation code and the INLA model results. The fixed
> effect parameters look OK. Since the random effect of the slope
> parameters are defined as rnorm(…,0,1), I would expect the precision
> hyper parameters to be ~1, but in almost all cases they are <<1. I
> tried some alternative priors, but that doesn’t seem to change much.
>
> Does anyone has an idea why the precision parameter estimates seem to
> be different from 1? Or do I miss-specify the model or
>  miss-interpreted the results?
>
> And a side question: Any suggestions on what would be the most
> appropriate prior distribution for the example below is very much
> appreciated.
>

you seems to doing it all correct. however, your estimates for the
precisions are highly sensitive for the prior chosen, so changing the
parameters to

formula = y ~ X1+X2+X3+X4+
    f(id1,X1,model="iid",prior="normal",param=c(1,1))+
    f(id2,X2,model="iid",prior="normal",param=c(1,1))+
    f(id3,X3,model="iid",prior="normal",param=c(1,1))+
    f(id4,X4,model="iid",prior="normal",param=c(1,1))

gives quite different results for the precisions.

the reason is that the binary data is weakly informative...

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thanks for the reply. Did try the suggestion, i.e. using more informative priors: ..prior="normal",param=c(1,1,)..., but somehow still receive precision estimates which are much smaller than 1 (in the order of .1 to .5). Also the standard deviation of the precision parameters are rather small (.03 to 0.1), which to me seems to suggests that precision estimates are truly different from 1.  Perhaps this is a more general consequence of fitting a Bayesian model, and has little to do with INLA…, don’t know.

At least it is good to know that my implementation is correct.

Cheers, Geert

On 27 June 2012 09:41, Victor <vale...@gmail.com> wrote:
> "good" conditioned here i presume notably the interior angle with respect to
> distance?

That is one part of it, yes; setting min.angle=26 is usually ok (the
triangulation algorithm is theoretically guaranteed to terminate for
min.angle<=21, but values as high as 30 often work in practice;
however, since there is a tradeoff between "nice" triangles and "few"
triangles, it's likely not worthwhile to use very large
min.angle-values).

> and in other words i have measurements that are very close in
> space which should not from a triangulation and these rather makes my matrix
> ill conditioned

Precisely; the size ratio between large and small triangles shouldn't
be too large.  Closely clustered sites with empty space in between are
among the worst offenders.

/Finn
